title: Estimating with Decimals
short: Round first to check where the decimal point belongs.
trouble: Students accept 2.4 × 3.1 = 74.4 because they never compare it with 2 × 3.

blocks.html: You can multiply decimals and round them. Put the two together and you have a fast check that catches a decimal point in the wrong place.
Round each factor to a whole number (or another easy number) and multiply. The exact answer should be close to the estimate. Use the estimate to place the decimal point.

The digits of $2.4 \times 3.1$ are the digits of $24 \times 31 = 744$. Where does the point go: $0.744$, $7.44$, $74.4$? Since $2.4$ is about 2 and $3.1$ is about 3, the product is about $2 \times 3 = 6$. Only $7.44$ is close to 6.

blocks.name: numberline
blocks.cap: The estimate, about 6, sits right next to $7.44$. $0.744$ is far below it, and $74.4$ would be far off the right end of this line.

blocks.title: Place the point
blocks.q: $3.8 \times 5.2$ has the digits 1976. Where does the point go?

blocks.title: Is it reasonable?
steps: $0.48$ is about $0.5$, a half, and $9.6$ is about 10.
Half of 10 is 5. $46.08$ is far from 5.

blocks.html: Accepting an answer like $2.4 \times 3.1 = 74.4$ without comparing it to $2 \times 3$. Check every decimal product with a whole-number estimate; a misplaced point is off by 10 times or more, which an estimate shows right away.
